intro: Bamberg's protected trees are not headline giants: four of the five carry no measured age at all, and the city's register describes most in a single line. What they have is genuine public ground: a spring path above Wildensorg, a roadside lane, a demolished manor's site, a riverbank downstream, and further out toward Teuchatz, a lime thick enough that people once thought it was three trees fused together. If you carry a tape measure, we would like to hear from you.
meta_description: Five protected Bamberg trees: two limes by a hillside spring, a roadside oak, a lime on a demolished manor's site, and a legend-dated lime near Teuchatz.
question_answer: The closest thing to a dated tree is the Great Lime of Teuchatz, well outside the city itself, whose girth points to something like 350 to 400 years if a local legend about its planting is right: soldiers buried here during the Thirty Years' War, sometime in the 1630s. None of Bamberg's other four protected trees carries any age estimate at all. The city's own register gives only a location and a protected status for those four. If you know how old any of Bamberg's five actually are, tell us.
question_meta: Bamberg's register protects five trees; the closest to a dated one is a lime near Teuchatz, its girth suggesting 350 to 400 years by legend.
question_context: Bamberg's Naturdenkmal-Verordnung, passed in November 1995 and amended in 2007, protects trees across the city and its outskirts and dates almost none of them. Each register entry carries a number, a common name, a location and the fact of protection, nothing about planting dates or growth. The five trees here were cross-checked against Wikipedia's reproduction of the register and geotagged Commons photographs. Three of the first four stand within a kilometre and a half of each other on the hillside above Wildensorg: two limes by a spring, an oak on the Teufelsgraben, and a lime on a demolished manor's site. The fourth stands alone by the Regnitz in Bug. None of those four carries a girth measurement. The fifth, the Great Lime of Teuchatz, stands sixteen kilometres out on a road with no rail and no confirmed bus, documented instead by a dedicated Wikipedia article citing published dendrology surveys, and it is the only one of the five anyone has ever measured: 770 centimetres round in 1990, 822 in 2008.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Bamberg?
faq.a: The best estimate belongs to the Great Lime of Teuchatz, a satellite tree well outside Bamberg, whose girth points to somewhere between 350 and 400 years if a local legend about its planting during the Thirty Years' War is right. None of the trees standing within the city itself has been dated at all.

faq.q: Can I see all five trees in one walk?
faq.a: No. Three, the Ottobrunnen lindens, the Teufelsgraben oak and the Rothof linden, sit within about a kilometre and a half of each other on the Wildensorg hillside. The Buger Hof linden is a separate trip a few kilometres away on the Regnitz. The Great Lime of Teuchatz is sixteen kilometres out and needs a car; it has no public transport connection to the city at all.

Four stand in the open with no gate: a footpath, two roadside verges and a quiet country road near Teuchatz. The Buger Hof linden stands at the edge of a riverside hotel's grounds; the view from the public towpath is free, and whether the ground directly beneath it is open was not confirmed.

faq.q: Why do so few of Bamberg's protected trees carry an age?
faq.a: The city's Naturdenkmal register records a number, a name, a location and the fact of protection, nothing about planting dates or ring counts, and that covers four of the five. The fifth, the Great Lime of Teuchatz, is documented separately in published dendrology surveys that give an actual girth history, which is where its rough age estimate comes from.

trees.name: The Lindens of the Ottobrunnen

location.address: Opposite the Ottobrunnen, off the Bamberger Weg footpath, Wildensorg (Berggebiet), Bamberg

trees.access: Free. Stands right beside a public footpath (Bamberger Weg) in the wooded Berggebiet above Wildensorg; reachable on foot or by Bamberg city bus toward Wildensorg Mitte (lines 910/913), then a short uphill walk.
trees.transport: Bus to Wildensorg Mitte (lines 910/913) then approx. 10-15 min uphill on foot; no train option.
trees.story:
Two trees, one monument. Bamberg's natural monument register lists number three as "2 Linden am Ottobrunnen", a pair of small-leaved limes on the wooded hillside above Wildensorg, and protects them as a single entry rather than as two trees that happen to stand together. They face the Ottobrunnen, a spring on the Bamberger Weg, the footpath that climbs out of the city into the Berggebiet. The well carries the name of Otto of Bamberg, the bishop who died in 1139. That name belongs to the water and to the ground around it, and nothing on record attaches these two limes to him, so the story stops where the sources do.

A lime beside a well is one of the older arrangements in German village life, the tree marking the water and the meeting place at once. Whether that is why this pair is here, nobody wrote down. What is written down is the protection: both fall under the city ordinance of November 1995, amended in 2007, which means neither can be felled or cut back at anyone's convenience.

Go for the walk rather than for the trees alone. The path is wooded, the climb is short, and the pair stands at the top of it with the spring opposite.

Neither lime has been dated and neither trunk has been measured. If you get up there with a tape, tell us what they come to.
trees.how_to_recognise: The pair of limes stands opposite a spring right where the Bamberger Weg footpath emerges from the trees; there is no other planted pair nearby.

trees.name: The Oak of the Teufelsgraben

location.address: Teufelsgraben, southwest of the Kaiser-Heinrich-Gymnasium, Wildensorg (Berggebiet), Bamberg

trees.access: Free, standing along the Teufelsgraben path/street on the Wildensorg hillside, southwest of the Kaiser-Heinrich-Gymnasium school; OpenStreetMap independently tags it as a roadside tree rather than inside a fenced plot. Not on school grounds; the register describes it as standing 'southwest of' the school, not on its site.
trees.transport: Uphill from central Bamberg in Wildensorg/Berggebiet; reachable by Bamberg city bus toward Wildensorg, then on foot.
trees.story:
The address is the Devil's Ditch. Teufelsgraben is a lane running down the Wildensorg hillside southwest of the Kaiser-Heinrich-Gymnasium, and the oak stands on the verge of it, in the open, with nothing between it and the lane. It is not a school tree. The register places it southwest of the building rather than on the site, and you reach it without passing a gate or asking anyone.

Worth knowing before you go: a second protected oak stands close by, and that one is inside a garden plot, which the register says in as many words. The tree on this page is the one out on the bank above the lane, standing alone.

It is a pedunculate oak, the species that hangs its acorns on long stalks and holds its leaves almost stalkless against the twig, which is the reverse of the sessile oak it gets confused with. Bamberg protects it as natural monument 5, under the ordinance the city passed in November 1995 and amended in 2007, so it cannot be felled or cut back at anyone's convenience.

The rest of the hillside is worth the climb with it. The Ottobrunnen limes and the lime at the old Rothof are both within a couple of kilometres on foot.

What nobody has recorded is how old this oak is or how thick. Oaks carry centuries without advertising them. If you have measured it, tell us.

photo.attribution: Stephan van Helden, via Wikimedia Commons

trees.how_to_recognise: A lone oak on the open verge of the Teufelsgraben lane, standing free of any fence or garden. A second protected oak on the same register sits inside a garden plot nearby and is not this one.

trees.name: The Linden of the Buger Hof

location.address: Am Regnitzufer 1, Bug, Bamberg (beside the Buger Hof hotel-restaurant, on the Regnitz riverbank)

trees.access: Free to view from the Regnitz riverside path; the address (Am Regnitzufer 1) is the Buger Hof hotel-restaurant, so the tree stands at the edge of its grounds beside the public riverbank. Whether a visitor needs to be a guest to stand directly beneath it, versus viewing it from the towpath, was not separately confirmed this pass; flagged so a future pass or reader can settle it.
trees.transport: In Bug, on the Regnitz river a few km south of central Bamberg; reachable by bike path along the river or by car/bus toward Bug.
trees.story:
Its official name is a house number. Bamberg's register of natural monuments lists entry 10 as "1 Linde am Regnitzufer 1", and the address it is named after is the Buger Hof, a hotel and restaurant on the riverbank in Bug, the village district a few kilometres upstream of the cathedral. The tree is a small-leaved lime and it stands at the edge of that ground, where the garden meets the Regnitz.

So the access is an open question and it is better said than glossed over. The lime is in full view from the public path along the river, the one walkers and cyclists use to get out of Bamberg southwards, and that view is free to anyone. Whether the last few metres underneath it are open to a passer-by or belong to the terrace is something we have not been able to settle. Look from the path. Ask inside if you want to stand under the crown.

Riverbank suits a lime better than almost anywhere else in a city: water at the root, open light on the water side, and no pavement compacting the ground over it. The city has protected this one since the ordinance of November 1995.

No age is recorded for it and no one has put a tape around the trunk. If you know either number, or whether the ground beneath it is open, tell us.

photo.attribution: Stephan van Helden, via Wikimedia Commons

trees.how_to_recognise: The lime at the corner of the Buger Hof's riverside grounds, visible from the towpath where the garden meets the Regnitz.

trees.name: The Linden of the Old Rothof

location.address: Wildensorger Straße, at the site of the former Rothof estate, Wildensorg (Berggebiet), Bamberg

trees.access: Free. The historic Rothof estate building itself was demolished in the mid-1960s (per infranken.de reporting on the site's later redevelopment as a municipal water reservoir); the property is no longer a private residence, and OpenStreetMap tags the tree as a roadside lime on Wildensorger Straße rather than inside a fenced garden. Treated as publicly reachable on that basis.
trees.transport: Uphill from central Bamberg in Wildensorg/Berggebiet; reachable by Bamberg city bus toward Wildensorg, then on foot.
trees.story:
The estate this tree is named after was pulled down in the middle of the 1960s. The Rothof stood on the Wildensorger Straße, up on the hillside west of Bamberg; the buildings went, and the ground eventually went to the city's drinking water, which is what the site holds now. The lime is still there, on what the register calls the northern boundary of the property. A boundary line with nothing left to divide.

That whole history is in the register's own wording. Natural monument 6, protected under the city ordinance of November 1995: "1 Linde am ehemaligen Rothof, nördliche Grundstücksgrenze". One lime at the former Rothof, northern property line. The farm is described in the past tense and the tree is not.

It is a small-leaved lime and it stands by the road, which is the useful part for anyone walking up: no gate, no garden, no permission. The hillside route that takes in the Teufelsgraben oak and the pair of limes at the Ottobrunnen passes within about a kilometre and a half of it, so all three fit into one afternoon on foot.

How much of the Rothof this lime actually saw is the open question. Nobody has dated it and nobody has measured the trunk. If you have, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: A lime standing alone by the road on Wildensorger Strasse, on open ground where the Rothof once stood. There is no building left to mark the spot beyond the tree itself.

trees.name: The Great Lime of Teuchatz
trees.age_estimate: roughly 350 to 400 years, if a local legend about its planting holds

location.address: On the road (Kreisstrasse) from Teuchatz to Burggrub, Markt Heiligenstadt in Oberfranken, Landkreis Bamberg

trees.access: Free. Stands immediately beside the public road between Teuchatz and Burggrub, no gate or fence.
trees.transport: About 16 km from Bamberg centre in the Fraenkische Schweiz, roughly 25 minutes by car. No rail (the branch line to Heiligenstadt closed in 1968) and no confirmed public bus reaches Teuchatz, so this one needs a car rather than the city's transit network.
trees.story:
Local legend ties this lime to the Thirty Years' War: soldiers from the Swedish army, the story goes, were buried here in the 1630s and the tree grew from their graves. Nobody can prove the burial, but the tree's girth roughly fits that timeline, tracked at 770 centimetres round in 1990 and 822 centimetres in 2008, which is honest grounds for guessing it is nearing four centuries old if the legend holds and nothing more precise if it does not.

The trunk is thick enough that a separate story grew up around it too, that it is really three trees fused into one. Look closely and the case falls apart. Dendrologists who have studied the tree describe a single continuous trunk, heavily buttressed and studded with burls at the base rather than three obvious stems. What has needed real intervention is the crown, cut back hard in recent years and now held together with steel cables above the point, about four metres up, where it forks into several broad limbs. It once spread 26 metres wide.

Teuchatz has no railway; the branch line that served it closed in 1968, and no confirmed bus makes the trip either. Getting here from Bamberg means a car and about 25 minutes on quiet roads, at the end of which the tree stands directly on the roadside with nothing between the pavement and the trunk. A war grave for a legend and a trunk that still argues about how many trees it started as.
trees.how_to_recognise: The one large lime standing directly on the roadside between Teuchatz and Burggrub, its crown visibly cut back and braced with steel cables; there is no other tree of its size on this stretch of road.
